title: Krishna Visits Shrutadeva and Bahulashva
story:
Two men in Mithila were preparing to receive the same guest, and neither had the faintest idea that the other was preparing as well.

Krishna, the lord of the Yadavas, was traveling through the land with a company of sages, and word of his coming ran ahead of him like wind. Mithila was proud of its wise kings and its courteous people; its boast was that no guest had ever been turned away hungry from its gates. The news reached two houses. One was the home of Shrutadeva, a brahmana — a scholar and priest — who had spent his life in study and worship and whose only wealth was his learning and his faith. The other was the palace of Bahulashva, king of Mithila, who ruled from a hall of pillars and whose storehouses could have bought half a kingdom.

The two men had little in common, but each heard that the teacher of the world was coming to Mithila, and each took it for granted that the visit was meant for him alone. To Shrutadeva it seemed plain that such a guest would honor a house of prayer; to Bahulashva it seemed just as plain that a king's palace was where such a guest belonged. Each set his whole household to work — the brahmana swept his courtyard and laid out his best food, the king hung garlands through his hall and sent for musicians. Each invited Krishna and the sages to stay, and neither thought to ask whether anyone else had invited them too.

Krishna understood both hearts, and he wished to please both. When he came into Mithila with the sages, the people of the city poured out to see him pass. At the palace gates the king went out to meet the travelers, weary as they were from the long road, his eyes blurred with tears; with his whole family he bowed low before Krishna and the sages and worshipped them.

"Your promise is kept," he said, his voice shaking. "Our eyes have rested on you at last. Stay in our house for a few days — you and the brahmanas with you."

And in that same hour, across the city, the same guest was seated in the brahmana's house. Shrutadeva had spread his plain mat, set before Krishna whatever his home possessed, and bowed and worshipped with the same overflowing joy. His hands had trembled as he laid out the meal; he had rehearsed his welcome for days, and the words had failed him — and it had not mattered, because Krishna accepted what was offered and was pleased.

So Krishna was whole in both houses at once — fully present at the king's table, fully present at the poor man's hearth — and neither host saw the other, and neither knew. One house fed its guests at a king's table; the other, at a brahmana's fire; and both tables served the same guest.

Night fell on Mithila. Two lamps burned — one beneath the pillars of the palace, one on the mud wall of the brahmana's room — and beneath each lamp sat the same guest, and each host's heart was full to the brim. The king slept that night as he had not slept in years; the brahmana slept the same.

Neither man ever learned the truth, and perhaps that too was part of the grace: each received all of Krishna, and neither one's joy was less because another's was equal. When morning came, both houses rose blessed, each family telling the story of the night, each certain it had been the only one.
reflection: Krishna honors the brahmana's hermitage and the king's palace with the same complete presence, and the wonder of the episode is that neither man's joy costs the other anything. Devotion is not measured by station, and grace is not rationed: the same Lord sits whole in a palace hall and in a thatched room, and each host receives all of him.
next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, however, a grief was gathering at the palace gate that no courtly joy could answer.
hero_scene: Night over Mithila: in the lamplit hall of King Bahulashva's palace, the king and his family bow low before Krishna, seated among the sages with tear-filled eyes — while across the city, in the brahmana Shrutadeva's thatched room, the same Krishna is visible seated on a simple mat, receiving the brahmana's offering under a second lamp.
